Description
I am looking to fill a fully funded PhD assistantship in the College of Forestry, Wildlife, and Environment at Auburn University, beginning January or May, 2027. Research in the Willoughby lab broadly examines how genetic and genomic variation shapes the persistence, evolution, and health of wild populations. Our work combines whole-genome sequencing, bioinformatics, experiments, and quantitative modeling to address questions in conservation genetics, evolutionary biology, and disease ecology. Additional information about our research and lab group is available on the Willoughby Lab website (https://willoughbylab.auburn.edu).
 The student will contribute to a newly funded project investigating brown-spot needle blight, an emerging threat to loblolly pine forests and timber production in the southeastern United States. This project continues a large interdisciplinary effort to characterize the fungi associated with the disease and understand its effects on pine growth and forest ecology. The student’s research will examine how genomic characteristics of pine-associated fungi, their responses to environmental stress, and fungal community composition contribute to variation in disease severity. The research will likely combine whole-genome sequencing, controlled experiments, RNA sequencing, and predictive modeling. The student will gain experience in fungal culturing, comparative genomics, bioinformatics, gene-expression analysis, and the integration of genomic, environmental, and ecological data. The precise emphasis of the dissertation can be shaped around the student’s interests within the broader goals of the funded project.
 The project is part of a large, interdisciplinary collaboration involving forest pathologists, geneticists, spatial scientists, extension specialists, graduate and undergraduate students, and scientists from Auburn University and the U.S. Forest Service. The ability and willingness to communicate across disciplines will therefore be important. The student should be interested in learning both laboratory and computational approaches and in connecting fundamental biological questions with an applied forest-health problem. Previous experience with molecular laboratory methods, fungal biology, genomics, bioinformatics, statistics, or programming is desirable, but applicants are not expected to arrive with experience in all—or even most—of these areas. Please do not self-select yourself out of applying. There are many ways to acquire the skills needed for a successful graduate experience, and the position is designed to provide training across laboratory, computational, and quantitative components of the research. More important qualifications include intellectual curiosity, persistence, a willingness to learn unfamiliar methods, clear communication, and the ability to work both independently and as part of a collaborative team.
 Auburn University is a very high research activity institution located in a mid-sized community in east-central Alabama. Auburn and neighboring Opelika offer a relatively low cost of living, restaurants, farmers markets, community events, and the Gogue Performing Arts Center. The nearby Kreher Preserve and Nature Center, Tuskegee National Forest, and other public lands provide year-round opportunities for outdoor recreation. Graduate students in the College of Forestry, Wildlife, and Environment receive a competitive stipend, tuition remission, and opportunities for professional development.
 I will interview prospective students before they submit a formal application to Auburn’s graduate program. Interested candidates should email Dr. Janna Willoughby at jwilloughby@auburn.edu with: 1) a brief description of their background and research interests;
2) an explanation of why this project interests them; and a PDF of their CV.
 Informal inquiries are welcome. Applications will be evaluated on a rolling basis and interviews are likely to occur no later than October 1, 2026.
Contact
Janna Willoughby
jwilloughby@auburn.edu (preferred contact method)

 Ph.D. Graduate Assistantship in Aquaculture Economics and Marketing

A Ph.D. graduate assistantship is available beginning Spring 2027 in the Department of Rangeland, Wildlife and Fisheries Management at Texas A&M University under the supervision of Dr. Shraddha Hegde.

The student will pursue a Ph.D. in Rangeland, Wildlife and Fisheries Management, with research focused on aquaculture economics and seafood marketing.

Research

The student will work on a seafood marketing project examining U.S. consumer preferences and purchasing behavior for domestic farm-raised seafood. Research will focus on identifying consumer segments with strong preferences for domestic farm-raised seafood and examining consumer information sources, values, and retail decision-making to inform effective marketing strategies for U.S. aquaculture producers.

The student will gain experience in survey research, quantitative and econometric analysis, manuscript preparation, and conference presentations.

We are particularly interested in applicants who are curious, proactive, enthusiastic about research, and willing to learn.

Assistantship

The position provides a $24,000 annual stipend, full tuition support, and funding for three years. Health insurance benefits are available according to university policy. The student may serve as a Teaching Assistant for one to two semesters as part of their teaching and professional development.

How to Apply

Please email the following to Dr. Shraddha Hegde at shraddha@tamu.edu:

Description
The Coastal Conservation and Restoration Lab at the Harte Research Institute for Gulf of Mexico Studies (HRI), Texas A&M University–Corpus Christi (TAMU-CC), is recruiting a PhD student to investigate how oyster reef restoration and management influence reef condition and ecological function in Texas. The anticipated start date is Summer or Fall 2027.

The student will join a newly funded, multi-year research project conducted in collaboration with resource managers and research partners. The project will compare natural, restored, and actively managed oyster reefs to understand how restoration and management practices influence oyster populations, reef structure, and ecological function.

The PhD student will have substantial opportunities to develop and take ownership of dissertation questions within this broader framework. Potential research directions include oyster population and reef dynamics; restoration ecology; relationships between reef structure and ecological function; effects of restoration and harvest management; habitat support and associated macrofaunal communities; and development of ecological indicators and thresholds for oyster reef monitoring and management.

Field research will include quantitative diver surveys and standard dredge sampling to characterize oyster density, size structure, mortality, and live and dead shell. Research will compare these measures among natural, restored, and actively managed reefs and evaluate whether routine fishery-monitoring metrics can provide useful indicators of broader reef condition and ecological function. Additional research will evaluate macrofaunal communities and habitat support.

Qualifications: Applicants should have demonstrated research experience and a strong interest in oyster reef ecology, restoration ecology, benthic ecology, fisheries, or coastal science. We are particularly interested in students who enjoy taking ownership of research questions, work well both independently and collaboratively, and approach research challenges with initiative, persistence, and creative problem-solving.

An M.S. degree in marine science, ecology, biology, fisheries, environmental science, or a related field is preferred but not required for applicants with substantial equivalent research experience. Experience with field research, oyster or benthic ecology, quantitative analysis/R, scientific writing, small-boat fieldwork, or scientific diving is beneficial but not required. SCUBA certification and scientific diving experience are preferred but not required.

The successful applicant will pursue a PhD through the Coastal and Marine System Science (CMSS) or Marine Biology (MARB) program at TAMU-CC and will be based at HRI in Corpus Christi, Texas. The project will involve substantial field research in Galveston Bay.

Funding: The position includes a graduate research assistantship with a stipend of $2,000/month, increasing to $2,200/month upon advancement to candidacy, plus tuition, required fees, and health insurance.

To apply: Email Dr. Jennifer Beseres Pollack at jennifer.pollack@tamucc.edu with (1) a CV, (2) unofficial transcripts, and (3) a brief email describing your research background and interests and why this opportunity interests you. Review of applications will begin immediately. For full consideration, materials should be received by December 15, 2026; the position will remain open until filled.

Jennifer Pollack

The Coastal Conservation and Restoration Lab and the Coastal Water Health Lab at the Harte Research Institute for Gulf of Mexico Studies (HRI), Texas A&M University–Corpus Christi (TAMU-CC), are recruiting a Ph.D. student to investigate how changing freshwater inflows influence water quality and estuarine ecosystems along the Texas coast. The anticipated start date is Summer or Fall 2027.

The student will join a newly funded, multi-year project evaluating environmental flows across Texas. The project combines a statewide assessment of post-Senate Bill 3 environmental flows with intensive ecological and water-quality monitoring in the Nueces Estuary, providing opportunities to investigate questions spanning coast-wide patterns to local ecological responses.

The Ph.D. student will have substantial opportunities to develop and take ownership of dissertation questions within this broader framework. Potential research directions include coast-wide patterns in freshwater inflows and environmental-flow attainment; relationships among freshwater inflows, salinity, nutrients, primary productivity, water quality, and benthic communities; long-term ecological change; and development of biological indicators to support environmental-flow assessment and adaptive management.

Field research will include monthly water-quality sampling, quarterly benthic and sediment sampling, and targeted sampling following major freshwater inflow events or water-management changes. The student will also work with historical and contemporary environmental datasets to examine relationships among freshwater inflows, water quality, and ecological responses.

Qualifications: Applicants should have demonstrated research experience and a strong interest in estuarine or coastal science, including areas such as water quality, biogeochemistry, benthic ecology, or aquatic ecology. We are particularly interested in students who enjoy taking ownership of research questions, work well both independently and collaboratively, and approach research challenges with initiative, persistence, and creative problem-solving.

An M.S. degree in marine science, ecology, biology, environmental science, or a related field is preferred but not required for applicants with substantial equivalent research experience. Experience with field research, water-quality monitoring, benthic ecology, quantitative analysis/R, scientific writing, or environmental datasets is beneficial but not required.

Description
As part of the Collaborative Forest Landscape Restoration Program, the Forest Service and its partners are using silviculture and prescribed fire to restore historical forest structure and composition in the northern Blue Mountains of Oregon and Washington within the Wallowa Whitman and Umatilla National Forests. To monitor restoration effects, the Pacific Northwest Research Station uses noninvasive methods (trail cameras and audio recording units) to measure wildlife responses to forest restoration treatments. These data provide landscape-scale information on species occurrence and habitat use, helping managers evaluate forest restoration outcomes and refine future treatments. This monitoring effort was initiated in 2022 and has been implemented annually across both National Forests, resulting in greater than a half a million hours of audio recordings and 150 thousand photos collected across more than 700 sites. For more information on this effort, please see the project webpage.

Wild turkeys were introduced to the region because (among other reasons) they are a popular game species. There is an interest in better understanding how gobbling activity varies across the region and time to better understand nesting phenology and wild turkey status and trends. There is also interest in understanding how turkeys respond to habitat treatments and if there is preference to one treatment over another. The western U.S.A. has a larger portion of public lands; therefore, understanding how turkeys respond to management activities in this region is vital to protecting public lands and public recreational activities that include hunting opportunities.

We are recruiting an MS student to leverage current and future data collected as part of this monitoring program to 1) quantify spatial, temporal, and annual dynamics in wild turkey gobbling activity across the Wallowa-Whitman and Umatilla National Forests, and 2) evaluate the effect of forest conditions (i.e., composition and structure), local weather conditions, and management activities (i.e., commercial thinning, non-commercial thinning, and prescribed fire) on wild turkey habitat use.

Although the student will primarily be located in Raleigh, NC, the position will involve extensive fieldwork conducted in northern Blue Mountains in the Pacific Northwest for at least one summer field season. Applicants must have a good driving record and be able to use good judgement when navigating on Forest Service roads. They should also have the necessary skills and experience to safely hike in remote forests off trail up to 10 miles a day, possibly gaining up to 4000 ft in elevation, carrying up to 35 lbs.

When working on campus, the work will require extensive amounts of time listening to audio recordings, processing trail camera photos, and analyzing data. The successful candidate will work under the direct supervision of Dr. Ivana Mali (North Carolina State University) in close collaboration with Dr. Adam Duarte (USDA Forest Service Pacific Northwest Research Station). The successful candidate is also expected to hold regular meetings with cooperators at the USDA Forest Service, National Wild Turkey Federation, and Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife to provide progress updates and receive feedback. Excellent command of the English language and a strong interest in learning quantitative analytical skills is absolutely required.

The position is expected to last from January 2027 to December 2028 (2 years). Student stipend is $25k annually. Additionally, in-state tuition will be covered. For domestic students who are not already residents of North Carolina, you are highly encouraged to establish North Carolina residency after the first two semesters, as Graduate Student Support Plan (GSSP) does not cover the out-of-state portion of the tuition after the first 2 semesters of enrollment. Please visit go.ncsu.edu/residency for current residency requirements. Please note that the system requires a minimum of 365 days of physical presence in North Carolina before you can apply, so non-residents should take action as early as possible toward establishing residency.

To apply, please send your CV and cover letter detailing your career goals and your interest in this project as a single PDF document to Dr. Mali (imali@ncsu.edu) and Dr. Duarte (adam.duarte@usda.gov). The deadline to apply is September 30, 2026.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is one of the major operation components of the Department of Health and Human Services. CDC works to protect America from health, safety and security threats, both foreign and in the U.S. Whether diseases start at home or abroad, are chronic or acute, curable or preventable, human error or deliberate attack, CDC fights disease and supports communities and citizens to do the same.

Research Project: The CDC National Center for Environmental Health (NCEH), Division of Environmental Health Science and Practice (DEHSP), Water, Food, and Environmental Health Services Branch (WFEHSB) is seeking a fellow to participate in environmental health workforce development and online course development activities. You will collaborate with CDC environmental health professionals and subject-matter experts to gain experience developing, reviewing, updating, and modernizing online training courses, educational materials, and practical tools for the environmental health workforce.

A central focus of the fellowship is training, under the guidance of a mentor, on the review and update of CDC's Environmental Health Training in Emergency Response (EHTER) course, including converting and enhancing content for online delivery. You will also collaborate to build tools and resources that support state, tribal, local, and territorial (STLT) environmental health professionals in routine practice and emergency preparedness/response. Activities include:
Gain experience reviewing and updating EHTER course content, learning objectives, exercises, and supporting training materials.

Position Overview

The Department of Forestry and Environmental Resources at NC State University invites applications for a fully funded 4-year Graduate PhD Research Assistantship starting January 1, 2027. The student will lead interdisciplinary research evaluating how site-specific silvicultural interventions—specifically fertilization and understory vegetation control—influence loblolly pine (Pinus taeda L.) growth, landscape yield response, and economic returns under market and input cost uncertainty across the southeastern US.

The selected candidate will work at the intersection of quantitative forest ecology, remote sensing, and resource economics, collaborating closely with industry partners from the Forest Productivity Cooperative (FPC) and the Southern Forest Resource Assessment Consortium (SOFAC).

Key Responsibilities & Project Objectives
Growth Response Modeling (Objective 1): Quantify the magnitude, duration, and uncertainty of pine growth responses to fertilizer and herbicide treatments across 100+ empirical field trial sites, integrating soil, geology, climate, and competing vegetation drivers.
Remote Sensing & Spatial Scaling (Objective 2): Build reproducible workflows using open-source platforms to map growth responses and understory vegetation across 550 million acres, leveraging satellite imagery and LiDAR.
Economic Risk & Decision Modeling (Objective 3): Conduct spatially explicit financial assessments. Develop regime-switching stochastic dynamic models to evaluate optimal management choices amid volatile input costs, shifting stumpage prices, and local market shocks (e.g., mill closures).
Science Communication: Author peer-reviewed publications, present research at professional conferences, and engage with regional forestry stakeholders.

Qualifications
Education: M.S. degree in Quantitative Forestry, Forest Biometrics, Geospatial Information Systems (GIS)/Remote Sensing, Forest Economics, Applied Statistics, Data Science, or a related natural resource discipline. Highly qualified applicants with a B.S. and strong quantitative research experience will also be considered.
Technical Skills:
◦ Strong programming experience (e.g., R, Python) for geospatial processing and statistical modeling.
◦ Experience working with remote sensing datasets (LiDAR, satellite imagery, raster analytics).
◦ Knowledge of econometric analysis, Monte Carlo simulation, dynamic programming, or spatial growth-and-yield modeling is preferred.
Communication: Track record of scientific writing and clear communication with diverse academic and practitioner audiences.

Advising Team
The student will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship from a multi-investigator team:
Dr. Rachel Cook – Professor of Silviculture & Forest Soils; Co-Director, Forest Productivity Cooperative (FPC)
Dr. Jeffrey Doser – Assistant Professor of Quantitative Forest Science
Dr. Justin Baker – Associate Professor of Forest Resource Economics; Director, Southern Forest Resource Assessment Consortium (SOFAC)

Funding & Compensation
Stipend: $30,000 / year (up to 4 full years of direct support, 2027–2030).
Tuition, Health Insurance & Expenses: Student fees, computing equipment, travel funding, and page charges are fully covered via PIs' matching funds and university programs.

How to Apply
Interested candidates should submit a single PDF document containing:

A 1–2 page cover letter detailing your research experience, quantitative background, and alignment with the project objectives.
Comprehensive Curriculum Vitae (CV).
Unofficial academic transcripts.
Contact information for three professional references.

Send applications to Rachel Cook (rlcook@ncsu.edu)
Include the following subject line: [Applicant Last Name] - PhD Application - Spatial Modeling of Forest Growth & Resource Economics

The PATHWAYS Program (Partnerships Along the Headwaters of the Americas for Young Scientists) is a National Science Foundation International Research Experience for Students (IRES), run jointly by Washington State University and the University of New Mexico. It places U.S. graduate students in interdisciplinary research on water and social-ecological systems across Central and South America. Student research topics can include watersheds, the downstream water-use systems, or the societies embedded in them, including the adaptation challenges posed by changing hydro-climatic conditions. Research on extraction and El Niño climate patterns will be a part of the program's focus this year. We're looking for students with an aptitude for interdisciplinary work and backgrounds in hydrologic science, engineering, ecology, or the social sciences.

The program runs over twelve months and combines online training with an in-person summer school in Cuenca, Ecuador and a funded research placement at a host institution in Central or South America:

• Spring training (Jan–Apr): online coursework and cohort-building
• Summer school in Cuenca, Ecuador (May): a mandatory two-week, in-person session grounded in real-world water-governance challenges
• International research experience (typically Jun–Aug): fieldwork at the student's chosen host institution
• Fall synthesis (Sep–Dec): online meetings and cross-case comparison, culminating in a research presentation to the network

Funding covers travel to and from the summer school and the research site, a subsistence stipend of $1,500/month during the international research experience, and support for research expenses.

To be eligible, applicants must be full-time graduate students who have not yet graduated and must be U.S. citizens, nationals, or permanent residents.

Description
 The Palmquist Lab at Marshall University is recruiting for an NSF funded MS position focused on evaluating the impacts of multiple global change drivers on dryland plant communities. Our research focuses on quantifying vegetation dynamics over space and time and identifying how the relative importance of ecological processes structuring plant communities changes with spatial and temporal scale. In addition, a key goal of our research is to understand how pattern and process in plant communities will be altered in the face of global environmental change. An important motivation for our work is to address ecological questions at large spatial scales to inform landscape conservation. We collect field data, use existing large observational data sets, and implement simulation modeling to address these goals in temperate shrublands, wetlands, woodlands, and forests. Additional information about the lab can be found at http://www.kylepalmquist.org/. 
 RESEARCH FOCUS: The successful candidate will broadly explore the interacting effects of climate change, wildfire, and livestock grazing intensity on big sagebrush plant communities throughout their spatial extent in the western US. These water-limited ecosystems are undergoing rapid environmental change due to multiple stressors (climate change, increases in wildfire activity, species invasions) and represent some of the most threatened systems in North America. This project is supported by a five-year NSF grant and will leverage an individual-based plant simulation model to quantify the impacts of multiple global change drivers on big sagebrush plant communities under future conditions. Potential focal projects the MS student would lead include: the role of competition in altering plant functional type responses to global change drivers and the implications for shrub-grass coexistence or leveraging livestock grazing as a tool to prevent the spread of invasive species and decrease wildfire risk under a future climate. This project will provide collaborative opportunities with ecologists at Yale University, and with scientists and managers from multiple federal agencies (BLM, USGS, USFWS, USFS, USDA ARS). 
 REQUIRED QUALIFICATIONS: A background and relevant course work in ecology and statistics, knowledge and experience in sagebrush ecosystems of the western U.S., strong communication skills, and strong quantitative skills. Experience in ecological modeling and computer programming is highly desirable. An interest in learning modeling is required. 
 EXPECTATIONS: The successful candidate will be expected to conduct high-quality research, serve as a teaching assistant within the Department of Biological Sciences for one year, present their research to the scientific community at regional and national meetings, and publish in peer-reviewed scientific journals.

 HOW TO APPLY: Interested students should apply by submitting the following to Dr. Kyle Palmquist (palmquist@marshall.edu): 1) short statement of research interests and career goals (no longer than 1 page), 2) CV, 3) unofficial transcripts, and 4) contact information for three professional references. Please include: “MS position - dryland plant communities” and your name in the email subject. 
 DEADLINE TO APPLY: No later than November 2, 2026. 
 Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until a candidate is selected. I will contact you to discuss your research interests and goals for graduate school if I determine you would be a good fit for the lab. If selected, a full application must be submitted to the Department of Biological Sciences at Marshall University, Huntington, WV. Faculty in the Department of Biological Sciences have expertise in a variety of biological fields, including but not limited to ecology, evolution, organismal biology, and physiology. More information about the Department and its programs can be found here: https://www.marshall.edu/biology/. The Conservation Genetics Lab at Boise State University, led by Dr. Stephanie Galla, is seeking a motivated graduate student to join the M.S. in Biology program through a National Science Foundation–funded research project.

The student will investigate the evolutionary history and conservation genetics of Sharp-tailed Grouse, using genomic data from both modern and historic specimens. The project will combine approaches in genomics, bioinformatics, evolutionary biology, and conservation biology to address questions about subspecies boundaries, population history, and changes in biodiversity through time.

Although the academic program will begin in Fall 2027, we intend for the applicant to begin research in May 2027 to advance their initial laboratory work over the summer. NSF Funding is available to pay for the summer work before fall semester begins.

Learn more about graduate study in Biology at Boise State University at this website here.

Project Description

The Intermountain West has experienced substantial habitat loss accompanied by declines in biodiversity. One subspecies of particular conservation concern is the Columbian Sharp-tailed Grouse (Tympanuchus phasianellus columbianus). Despite ongoing conservation efforts, important questions remain about the evolutionary history, population structure, and subspecific boundaries of Sharp-tailed Grouse.
This project will use genomic sequencing of modern and historic specimens from across the range of Columbian Sharp-tailed Grouse and other Sharp-tailed Grouse subspecies to investigate:

The evolutionary history of Sharp-tailed Grouse, including proposed subspecific boundaries
Changes in genetic diversity in Columbian Sharp-tailed Grouse over time 

The successful student will work closely with a collaborative team of scientists and will gain hands-on experience at the intersection of conservation genetics, genomics, bioinformatics, and evolutionary biology. The project offers opportunities to develop skills in laboratory methods, genomic data analysis, coding, and interpretation of genetic data for conservation and management.

Job Description

The Department of Forest Resources and Environmental Conservation at Virginia Tech invites applications for a tenure-track Assistant or Associate Professor position in Social Science and Sustainability. We seek a collaborative and innovative social scientist whose work addresses the human dimensions of sustainability with an emphasis on natural resource management, environmental conservation, and/or environmental governance. The specific topic of sustainability research is open, and we welcome diverse candidates whose substantive and methodological expertise complements and strengthens our program. This position will contribute to our department’s ongoing efforts to integrate rigorous social science into our interdisciplinary curriculum and research portfolio. The successful candidate must develop a productive externally funded research program and teach undergraduate and graduate courses in areas such as leadership for sustainability and other topics aligned with their expertise. Individuals must have a PhD in a social science field relevant to sustainability.

Job responsibilities will include:

Research (50%)
• Develop and maintain a robust, externally funded research program focused on the human dimensions of sustainability.
• Engage in interdisciplinary collaboration across campus and with external stakeholders, such as natural resource agencies, NGOs, and community organizations.
• Advise and mentor graduate students.

Teaching (50%)
• Teach 2–3 courses per academic year relevant to the Environmental Conservation & Society major, with a specific expectation to teach “FREC 2554 Leadership for Global Sustainability”
• Contribute to curriculum development and departmental service.

About the Department of Forest Resources and Environmental Conservation
The Department of Forest Resources and Environmental Conservation at Virginia Tech is one of the top forestry, natural resource management, and conservation programs in the United States. Our vision, mission, and values statements can be found here: https://frec.vt.edu/vision_mission_values.html. We are an inclusive and collaborative department that values knowledge and innovation; ethics and integrity; diversity and inclusivity; opportunity and affordability; and sustainability. Our exceptional education, research, and outreach programs are diverse and approach critical natural resource issues from many perspectives. The department offers master's and doctoral programs, as well as five undergraduate majors: environmental conservation and society, environmental data science, environmental resource management, forestry, and water resources policy and management. Faculty research areas of focus include forest biometrics, modeling, and remote sensing; forest biology, physiology, and genomics; ecology, silviculture, and wildland fire; hydrology, soils, and watershed management; forest management, operations, and business; resource economics and policy; human dimensions of natural resources and sustainability; environmental education, interpretation, and communication; and urban forestry. Department faculty also are engaged with industrial cooperatives, as well as extension and outreach efforts such as landowner education, SHARP logger, Master Naturalist, learning networks focused on environmental education and interpretation, and geospatial education programs.

Required Qualifications

• PhD by appointment date in a social science field relevant to sustainability, natural resource management, or a closely related field.

Preferred Qualifications

• Demonstrated commitment to or excellence in teaching or designing courses related to environmental sustainability at the undergraduate and graduate levels.
• Demonstrated potential for, or success in, securing external funding to support research.
• A record of high-quality research and publication in relevant fields.
• Methodological expertise that complements existing departmental strengths and enhances opportunities for interdisciplinary research and external funding. Relevant expertise may include quantitative, qualitative, mixed-methods, computational, spatial, participatory, or other rigorous social science approaches.
• Ability to work across disciplinary and methodological boundaries.

Understanding the important targets within the network of processes involved in maintaining normal functioning thyroid hormone levels, and what approaches to best assess activity at those targets are critical to developing a comprehensive approach to evaluating thyroid hormone disrupting potential of large numbers of chemicals.

The Palmquist Lab at Marshall University is recruiting for a funded MS position at Marshall
University in vegetation dynamics and plant community change in coastal ecosystems. Our
research focuses on quantifying vegetation dynamics over space and time and identifying how
the relative importance of ecological processes structuring plant communities changes with
spatial and temporal scale. In addition, a key goal of our research is to understand how pattern
and process in plant communities will be altered in the face of global environmental change. An
important motivation for our work is to address ecological questions at large spatial scales to
inform landscape conservation. We collect field data, use existing large observational data sets,
and implement simulation modeling to address these goals in temperate shrublands, wetlands,
woodlands, and forests. Additional information about the lab can be found at
http://www.kylepalmquist.org/.

RESEARCH FOCUS: The successful candidate will explore plant community patterns and
short-term vegetation change and dynamics in coastal ecosystems on Marine Corps Recruit
Depot Parris Island (MCRDPI), a sea-island in South Carolina. Coastal vegetation provides
important ecosystem services, including storm protection, erosion control, and habitat for
wildlife. These complex, highly zoned plant communities are structured by multiple
environmental factors including salinity, elevation, soil texture, soil moisture, exposure, and light
availability. The project will leverage an existing network of 57 permanent vegetation plots
located throughout the island that were installed and sampled in 2022. The successful candidate
will re-sample these plots in summer 2027 to evaluate plant community change. In addition,
there is a rich plant community data set from 2022 that has yet to be fully explored. Finally, the
student will be able to leverage and potentially improve existing vegetation maps of the island
that were created from an integration of remotely sensed products and field validation points.

knowledge and experience with the vegetation of the southeastern US, strong communication
skills, and strong quantitative skills. Experience with plant community analysis and an interest in
questions that evaluate plant community patterns over space and time.

serve as a teaching assistant within the Department of Biological Sciences, present their research
to the scientific community at regional and national meetings, and publish in peer-reviewed
scientific journals.

Description
The Institute for Global Change Biology at the University of Michigan seeks a postdoctoral researcher for a regional biodiversity model intercomparison project (BMIP) examining diverse correlative, process-based, and hybrid biodiversity models for projecting species and population responses to climate and land-use change. The postdoctoral researcher will support the development and synthesis of the model intercomparison of the sModelProBio working group (led by Greta Bocedi, University of Aberdeen and Damaris Zurell, University of Potsdam). The sModelProBio working group represents a collaborative project of sDiv (Synthesis Centre of the German Center for Biodiversity, iDiv) and the Institute for Global Change Biology, funded under the multi-institutional Global Synthesis Call on “Interactions between Biodiversity and Climate Change”. The sModelProBio working group is made up of an international team of researchers from the University of Aberdeen, University of Potsdam, University of Connecticut, San Diego State University, the University of Michigan, and elsewhere. This effort fills a critical gap in biodiversity science by providing robust regional-scale projections required for conservation planning and policy implementation. The postdoc will be co-supervised by Peter Reich (Director of the IGCB) and sModelProBio leaders Damaris Zurell and Greta Bocedi.

We seek an outstanding candidate with strong computational and quantitative skills and training in ecology, biodiversity science, environmental science, or a related discipline. Candidates must have expertise in programming, including in R, and experience in ecological modelling. The successful candidate might also have experience in one or more of these areas: Bayesian modeling, ecological forecasting, simulation modeling, ecophysiological modeling, hybrid AI-mechanistic models, or related quantitative approaches.

The postdoctoral researcher will be a member of the working group, support the modelling case studies, develop reproducible analytical workflows, quantify sources of uncertainty, and contribute to biodiversity projections relevant to conservation planning and policy. Opportunities will exist to develop independent projects, receive training from multiple scientists, and contribute to international workshops. The candidate will work closely with an international network of biodiversity and climate scientists while helping to develop new approaches for linking regional biodiversity projections with broader-scale assessments. This position offers an opportunity to contribute to a highly collaborative synthesis effort at the forefront of biodiversity forecasting and global change ecology.

The successful applicant will have completed a PhD degree in ecology, biology, Earth sciences, computer science, or a related field prior to the start date. An excellent publication record, strong organizational and communication skills, and a demonstrated ability to work independently are required. Preference will be given to scientists with experience in ecological modeling, software or package development, and designing novel computational workflows.

Review of applications will begin September 1, 2026; applications will be considered until a candidate is hired. The initial appointment period will be for one year with the expectation of a single renewal pending satisfactory performance. The successful candidate will participate in a program that includes career mentoring, professional development, and academic networking opportunities. Applications must include: 1) a cover letter that explains your fit to the research position, what novel insights or skills you would add, and your potential start date; 2) a complete CV with publications and grants; and 3) PDF copies of at least three publications, and 4) letters from two references; please ask both to upload their letters here. Combine all other parts of the application into a single PDF and upload the file in the application form here. The Institute for Global Change Biology (IGCB) at the University of Michigan seeks a postdoctoral researcher to support an international synthesis project examining how climate change may reshape ecosystem functioning and evolutionary diversity through its effects on species distributions. The postdoctoral researcher will contribute to the development of analytical frameworks that integrate species distribution models, climate vulnerability assessments, functional traits, ecosystem services, and phylogenetic information to better understand biodiversity responses to global environmental change.


The position will support the Freshwater Futures Working Group, funded by the Canadian Institute of Ecology and Evolution (CIEE). The working group brings together an international team of researchers from the University of Regina, University of Toronto, McGill University, and Dalhousie University in Canada; the University of Michigan and the University of Vermont in the United States; the Federal University of Ceará and the Federal University of Pará in Brazil; and the Zoological Society of London in the United Kingdom. The group aims to develop open, reproducible tools for assessing the impacts of climate change on biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and evolutionary history, with a particular focus on freshwater ecosystems and biodiversity policy applications.


The successful candidate will be co-supervised by Dr. Thiago Gonçalves-Souza and Dr. Bruno Soares (University of Regina) and will work closely with an international network of ecologists, conservation scientists, and biodiversity policy experts. The position offers substantial opportunities to collaborate across institutions while developing independent research projects related to biodiversity forecasting, climate adaptation, and conservation planning.


We seek an outstanding candidate with strong computational and quantitative skills and training in ecology, biodiversity science, environmental science, geography, statistics, computer science, or a related discipline. Candidates must have strong quantitative programming skills and experience with ecological modeling and species distribution models (SDMs). Experience with biodiversity analyses, environmental data science, ecological forecasting, or climate change vulnerability assessments would be particularly valuable. Additional assets include experience with macroecology and biogeography, functional or phylogenetic diversity analyses, and the development of analytical tools, R packages, or dashboards.


The postdoctoral researcher will serve as a core member of the working group and will:

Support the development and synthesis of regional and large-scale biodiversity analyses.
Develop reproducible workflows integrating biodiversity, trait, climate, and phylogenetic datasets.
Quantify uncertainties associated with biodiversity projections and climate vulnerability assessments.
Contribute to the development of biodiversity indicators relevant to conservation planning and international biodiversity targets.
Lead and co-author peer-reviewed publications.

The candidate will work closely with scientists studying biodiversity change across multiple ecological systems while helping develop new approaches that connect biodiversity forecasts to ecosystem functioning, resilience, and conservation decision-making. This position provides a unique opportunity to contribute to a highly collaborative synthesis effort at the interface of global change ecology, biodiversity science, and environmental policy. The successful candidate will join a vibrant research community at the Institute for Global Change Biology and participate in mentoring, professional development, and international networking opportunities.
 
The successful applicant will have completed a PhD in ecology, biology, environmental science, geography, computer science, statistics, or a related field prior to the start date. An excellent publication record, strong communication and organizational skills, and demonstrated ability to work independently are required. Preference will be given to candidates with experience in ecological modeling, biodiversity forecasting, interdisciplinary synthesis projects, and computational tool development.


Review of applications will begin November 1, 2026 and continue until the position is filled. The appointment period will initially be for one year, with the possibility of extension pending satisfactory performance and funding availability.

A cover letter (maximum 1 page) describing the applicant's relevant research experience and explaining how their background, technical skills, and research interests align with the objectives of this postdoctoral project. Applicants should also briefly describe how they envision contributing to the project and indicate their anticipated start date.
A curriculum vitae, including publications and funding history.
PDF copies of up to three representative publications.
Contact information for three references.

Description
In the Department of Wildlife Sciences at the Faculty of Forestry Sciences and Forest Ecology, Georg-August-University Göttingen, the position of

Research Associate (f/m/d) 

is available as soon as possible within a third-party funded project focused on the further development of methods for genetic estimation of wildlife population sizes. The position is full-time (100% of regular weekly working hours, currently 39.8 hours per week). The position is initially limited until 30 June 2029, with the intention of extending it for a full three years. Remuneration is according to salary group 13 TV-L (this is the typical salary group for postdocs in Germany - it is enough money to live well). 
 

Position Description
In recent years, several methods for estimating wildlife population sizes based on the genetic identification of kinship relationships have been developed. These include, among others, Close-Kin Mark-Recapture (CKMR; see Sévêque et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14490) and approaches involving the reconstruction of pedigrees (see Rosenblatt et al. 2023,  https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.10650). The successful candidate will further develop existing methods and adapt them for application to wild species commonly found in Germany that are subject to hunting. The initial focus will be on red deer (Cervus elaphus) and other ungulates, for which genetic samples can be collected via hunting. 

In addition to methodological development, you will use simulations to test the applicability of the method(s) under realistic conditions, and implemented the most promising approaches in R. 

There is also the opportunity to collaborate with researchers in the USA to test the methodology on a solitary carnivore species.

 Your Profile
We are seeking a highly motivated, productive, and independent individual with strong quantitative skills, particularly in statistical modeling. You possess…

-  a completed master's or diploma degree in a scientific field in Statistics, Modeling, Ecology, Genetics, Biology, or a closely related field  
- experience in statistical model development and coding  
- experience with simulation models  
- basic knowledge of population ecology  
- basic knowledge of population genetics  
- solid programming skills in R  
- excellent spoken and written English skills  
- experience in scientific writing, demonstrated by (co-)authorship of peer-reviewed articles in scientific journals  
- strong interest in wildlife ecology  

Advantageous are: a PhD in a relevant field, experience in statistical estimation of wildlife abundance—particularly using genetic methods—experience in determining kinship relationships using genetic markers, and knowledge of, or interest in, hunting-related topics.

Place of work is Göttingen. 

We offer flexible working conditions with significant potential for personal development.  

The University of Göttingen aims to increase the proportion of women in areas where they are underrepresented and therefore strongly encourages qualified women to apply. The university considers itself family-friendly and promotes the compatibility of academic work and family life. The university is particularly committed to the professional integration of disabled employees and welcomes applications from disabled persons. In cases of equal qualifications, applications from disabled persons will be given preference. Disability or equivalent status should be indicated in the application to safeguard your interests.


Please submit your clear, English-language application (including CV, cover letter, and copies of key certificates or employment references) as a single, continuous PDF document by 30.09.2026 to Agnieszka Melzer (wildlife@gwdg.de ). In your cover letter, please emphasize your relevant statistical expertise and, if applicable, your experience in abundance estimation.

For any questions about the position, please contact Niko Balkenhol (nbalken@gwdg.de).

Note:

By submitting your application, you consent to the processing of your personal data by us in accordance with data protection regulations. For more information on the legal basis and data usage, please see: [Information Sheet on the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)](https://uni-goettingen.de/DSGVO)

Contact
Niko Balkenhol
nbalken@gwdg.de (preferred contact method)

POSITION SUMMARY
The accelerating effects of climate change are among the greatest obstacles to protecting and restoring wildlife at risk of extinction. The Center for Conservation Innovation (CCI) at Defenders of Wildlife is seeking an interdisciplinary leader to serve as Director of Climate Adaptation and help advance science-based strategies that address these challenges. 

Reporting to the Vice President of Conservation Research and Innovation, the Director is a leader within CCI responsible for guiding Defenders’ efforts to address the impacts of climate change on wildlife and ecosystems. The Director will manage a small team of scientists and policy analysts dedicated to aligning climate and biodiversity objectives to enhance the protection of at-risk species and their habitats across the United States. This includes applying climate science, social science, and policy analysis to develop innovative approaches to conservation planning and decision-making. 

The Director will lead and collaborate on applied research initiatives focused on understanding climate change impacts on wildlife and ecosystems, nature-based solutions, wildlife-compatible energy development, ecosystem resilience, and species adaptation. Working closely with CCI’s Conservation Science and Technology teams, as well as legal, field, and policy staff across the organization, the Director will ensure that the latest climate science and policy strategies are effectively integrated into Defenders’ conservation, advocacy, and field-based efforts.

The ideal candidate is a strategic thinker and an effective communicator with experience in leading interdisciplinary teams. They possess a strong background in climate adaptation and conservation, including expertise in ecological, social, or economic dimensions of conservation decision-making and have a demonstrated ability to bridge disciplines and engage diverse stakeholder groups. This individual is expected to think creatively, work collaboratively, and successfully advance innovative solutions to complex conservation challenges.

ESSENTIAL DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES

Leads and develops a team of scientists and analysts:
Oversees the planning, prioritization, and execution of the climate team’s portfolio of projects and initiatives, aligning work with organizational strategy. 
Supervises a small team of staff and occasional volunteers, providing strategic direction, mentorship, and accountability for successful project delivery.
Ensures direction from Defenders’ leadership, including the VP, is shared with and contextualized for supervisees.
Leads climate science and policy analyses to improve wildlife conservation:
Develops and oversees applied research and decision-support initiatives focused on climate vulnerability, socio-ecological systems, and conservation strategies that strengthen outcomes for imperiled species in the face of accelerating change.
Helps position Defenders to address emerging climate and biodiversity challenges through strategic analysis and development of innovative conservation approaches, technologies, and partnerships.
Guides interdisciplinary program teams in the strategic use of climate science, social science, and policy analysis.
Advises on development of next-generation conservation policy frameworks that respond to accelerating threats and anticipate ecological change.
Advances conservation through partnerships and collaboration:
Identifies opportunities for cross-programmatic collaboration across energy, human-wildlife co-existence, and biodiversity initiatives.
Builds strong working relationships across departments to promote communication, coordination, and shared conservation outcomes.
Cultivates and leads strategic partnerships with researchers, agencies, NGOs, Indigenous communities, and other stakeholders to develop and advance climate-informed conservation solutions. 
Communicates and shares results and conservation implications:
Translates complex data into actionable insights for policy, advocacy, and on-the-ground action.
Supports and advises on strategic communications, translating complex scientific information for diverse audiences and contributing to advocacy, media engagement, public outreach, and policymaker education.
Publishes project findings in peer-reviewed journals, reports, blogs, articles, and/or other media. Communicates findings at scientific conferences and other events.

Travel Requirements: up to 5% of the time.
Perform all other related duties as assigned.
 QUALIFICATIONS
Education: Advanced degree (MS/PhD) or equivalent (Master’s degree in relevant field or equivalent required)
 Experience: At least 8 years of relevant experience, including at least 3 years managing staff and leading complex interdisciplinary projects.
An equivalent combination of education and experience may be accepted as a satisfactory substitute for the specific education and experience listed above.
 Knowledge, Skills, Abilities for All Defenders 
https://defenders.org/knowledge-skills-and-abilities 
 Knowledge, Skills, Abilities for Director of Climate Adaptation
Deep expertise in climate science as it relates to impacts on wildlife, habitats, and ecosystem processes across terrestrial, freshwater, and/or marine systems.
Knowledge of federal and state conservation policies relevant to climate adaptation and species recovery as well as the social, economic, and governance factors that influence conservation outcomes. 
Demonstrated ability to develop and implement an applied research agenda, including by supervising scientists and analysts and leading collaborations with internal and external partners.
Ability to align research questions and workflows with broader organizational goals and needs.
Experience with climate modeling, downscaled projections, uncertainty analysis, and adaptation frameworks as well as scientific analysis methods such as population viability analysis, landscape prioritization, habitat connectivity analysis, climate vulnerability analyses, and socio-ecological systems analysis.
Skilled communicator able to convey complex scientific and policy information to diverse audiences, in writing, in presentations, and via compelling data visualizations and maps.
Demonstrated record of scientific leadership through peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, policy analyses, or other influential conservation products.
Experience using geospatial, statistical, and computational tools to inform conservation science and climate adaptation. Proficiency with GIS and R or Python strongly preferred; familiarity with remote sensing, machine learning, and artificial intelligence is desirable.
Interest and drive to pursue and develop innovative conservation ideas and tools. Enthusiasm for using data to catalyze and improve biodiversity conservation.

POSITION SUMMARY
Rapid advances in technology, from satellite remote sensing to artificial intelligence and predictive analytics, are transforming our ability to understand and protect wildlife. The Center for Conservation Innovation (CCI) at Defenders of Wildlife is seeking an innovative and collaborative leader to serve as Director of Conservation Technology and help harness these advances to scale conservation impact.

Reporting to the Vice President of Conservation Research and Innovation, the Director is a leader within CCI responsible for guiding Defenders’ efforts to leverage data science, technology, and innovation to advance species recovery, conservation planning, conservation monitoring, and evaluation of conservation outcomes. They will lead, develop, and work alongside a small team of scientists and developers applying environmental data science, artificial intelligence, remote sensing, and other emerging technologies to strengthen wildlife conservation. This includes setting the team’s strategic direction and overseeing the development of innovative analytical approaches, decision-support tools, and technology-enabled conservation solutions.

Working closely with Defenders’ field, policy, and legal staff, as well as agency partners and other conservation practitioners, the Director will identify priority challenges and opportunities for innovation. Serving as a bridge between conservation practitioners and the research and technology communities, they will help identify, adapt, and deploy practical solutions that improve conservation outcomes and integrate them into Defenders’ legal, policy, and field-based efforts.

The ideal candidate is an ambitious, entrepreneurial, and creative leader driven by the opportunity to translate data and emerging technologies into real-world conservation solutions. They are a strategic thinker and effective communicator with experience leading interdisciplinary teams, building partnerships, and connecting conservation challenges with practical, high-impact technology solutions.

ESSENTIAL DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
 Leads and develops a team of scientists and technologists: 
Oversees the planning, prioritization, and execution of the technology team’s portfolio of projects and initiatives.
Supervises and mentors a small team of scientists, application developers, and occasional volunteers, providing guidance, professional development, and accountability for successful project delivery.
Ensures direction from Defenders’ leadership, including the VP, is shared with and contextualized for supervisees.
Leads Defenders’ data science and conservation technology program:
Guides Defenders' approach to data science and emerging technologies, identifying opportunities and helping prioritize investments and applications that advance conservation goals and align with organizational priorities.
Serves as a bridge between conservation practitioners and the research and technology communities, connecting priority conservation challenges with innovative analytical and technology solutions.
Advances organizational approaches, partnerships, and policies that support the responsible use and scaling of innovative conservation technologies.
Develops and delivers data-driven conservation solutions:
Prototypes, develops, and deploys innovative tools, analyses, monitoring and evaluation systems, and decision-support resources that address wildlife conservation needs. 
Creates dashboards, visualizations, online applications, and other resources that communicate findings and support conservation practitioners. 
Translates technical concepts and findings for diverse audiences through communications, advocacy materials, media engagement, and public outreach.
Builds partnerships and advances collaboration:
Cultivates partnerships with conservation organizations, government agencies, Tribal partners, technology companies, and other stakeholders to advance shared conservation goals.
Represents Defenders at meetings, conferences, trainings, and other forums to share innovative approaches, strengthen partnerships, and facilitate adoption of CCI work products.

Travel Requirements: up to 5% of the time.
Perform all other related duties as assigned.

QUALIFICATIONS
Education: Advanced degree in a relevant field (e.g. masters) required; PhD preferred
Experience: At least 8 years of relevant experience, including at least 3 years managing staff and leading complex interdisciplinary projects.
 An equivalent combination of education and experience may be accepted as a satisfactory substitute for the specific education and experience listed above.
 Knowledge, Skills, Abilities for All Defenders
https://defenders.org/knowledge-skills-and-abilities

Knowledge, Skills, Abilities for Director of Conservation Technology

Required skills: 
Demonstrated experience applying data science, geospatial analysis, computational methods, software development, or related disciplines to address conservation planning, recovery, or monitoring challenges. 
Ability to listen to conservation practitioners, identify opportunities for innovation, and connect real-world challenges with practical, scalable analytical and technology-enabled solutions. 
Experience leading and developing technical teams, including supervising staff and managing applied research, analytical, or technology programs. 
Technical expertise in GIS, R/Python, large and complex datasets, cloud-based platforms, remote sensing imagery, and data visualization tools. Experience evaluating and applying artificial intelligence is highly desirable. 
Experience building partnerships and collaborating effectively with conservation practitioners, agencies, Tribal partners, academic institutions, technology organizations, and other stakeholders. 
Knowledge of the U.S. Endangered Species Act and other federal and state conservation policies relevant to species conservation, recovery, and management. 
Strong strategic planning and project management skills, including the ability to prioritize opportunities, align technical work with organizational goals, and manage multiple initiatives. 
Excellent written and verbal communication skills, including the ability to translate complex technical concepts and analytical findings for decision-makers, practitioners, policymakers, and the public.

Description
About Archbold
Archbold Biological Station is a distinctive nonprofit research, conservation, and education organization rooted in the landscapes of south-central Florida. Since 1941, Archbold has been dedicated to long-term ecological research, education, and conservation as part of the global effort to understand, interpret, and preserve the world’s natural heritage. Our work spans the globally significant ecosystems of the Lake Wales Ridge and Headwaters of the Everglades as well as Buck Island Ranch, a 10,300-acre working cattle ranch where science informs the future of Florida’s working lands. Across these landscapes, scientists, land stewards, educators, students, and partners work together to understand ecological change, conserve biodiversity, strengthen stewardship, and connect science with people and practical solutions.

Located in Lake Placid, Archbold offers the opportunity to live and work in a region renowned for its natural beauty and rural character. Lake Placid offers a distinctive quality of life in the heart of south-central Florida. Surrounded by lakes, ranchlands, and some of Florida’s most unique natural ecosystems, the area combines exceptional access to nature with the warmth of a small, friendly community. Away from the traffic and fast pace of Florida’s coastal cities, Lake Placid provides a quieter lifestyle while still offering an active local community and easy access to outdoor recreation throughout the region.

Position Summary
The Associate Director is a senior management leader who strengthens the people, management systems, and internal coordination that enable Archbold to carry out its mission effectively. Reporting to and working closely with the Executive Director & CEO, the Associate Director supervises a portfolio that includes archives, intern and volunteer coordination, communications, human resources, environmental education, event services, and facilities, translating organizational priorities into clear expectations, coordinated work, and follow-through.

People leadership is central to this position. Success depends on leading through capable managers and professionals rather than personally performing every function under the role's oversight. Archbold seeks a leader who manages with transparency, humility, clarity, and respect; listens well; supports appropriate autonomy and accountability; and helps people succeed. The role is based primarily at the Station but works across Archbold's diverse mission, including Buck Island Ranch, research, stewardship, working lands, education, outreach, and engagement.

Key Responsibilities
People Management & Leadership
Directly supervise managers and professionals who lead their respective functional areas, with additional staff working within those teams.
Establish clear roles, responsibilities, decision authority, performance expectations, and accountability aligned with organizational priorities.
Coach supervisors and staff in management, communication, performance, professional development, delegation, and appropriate autonomy.
Address personnel and operational challenges constructively and strengthen collaboration across teams.
Partner with Human Resources on hiring, onboarding, performance management, staff development, and consistent workplace practices.
Organizational Effectiveness & Execution
Oversee assigned administrative, engagement, and mission-support functions, ensuring managers and staff have the support and accountability needed to lead effectively.
Translate institutional priorities into clear work plans, ownership, timelines, and follow-through; identify gaps or barriers that impede effective work.
Improve systems, policies, workflows, and cross-functional coordination; track key decisions, commitments, and deadlines.
Provide supervisory oversight of maintenance and other operational functions by setting priorities, clarifying responsibility, supporting appropriate decision-making, and ensuring follow-through.
 Work with the Executive Director, CFO, and relevant managers on annual planning and budgeting for areas under the Associate Director’s oversight.
Mission Integration & Collaboration
Work closely with the Executive Director and leadership team to support implementation of organization-wide priorities and coordinate cross-functional initiatives within delegated areas.
Strengthen coordination among staff in stewardship, working lands, education, outreach, communications, and operations.
Support education, outreach, communications, and public-engagement staff so mission-facing work is coordinated and aligned with organizational priorities.
Provide clear, concise information and recommendations when executive decisions are needed.
Required Qualifications
Education
Bachelor’s degree in a relevant field, plus significant professional experience in organizational administration, operations, program management, or a related area.
Master’s degree or other advanced education is strongly preferred, or an equivalent combination of advanced education and progressively responsible professional experience.
Demonstrated success in organizational leadership, operational management, strategic planning, and/or program administration.
Experience
Substantial, progressively responsible administrative and management experience involving organizational operations, personnel management, program oversight, and coordination across multiple functions or teams.
Significant formal responsibility for directly supervising employees, including setting expectations, coaching, managing performance, supporting professional development, and fostering accountability.
Demonstrated ability to lead through other managers and professionals rather than personally performing all functions under their oversight.
Strong understanding of and appreciation for science and scientific research in a mission-driven organization. Research experience is not required, but candidates must be comfortable working closely with scientists in a culture where evidence and long-term knowledge are central.
Demonstrated understanding of the importance of education, outreach, communications, and public engagement. Experience leading, supervising, or working closely with one or more of these functions is strongly preferred.
Certifications/Licenses
None required

Preferred Qualifications
Experience in a nonprofit, research, educational, conservation, environmental, natural-resource, or similarly mission-driven organization; biological field-station familiarity is a significant advantage.
Experience overseeing multiple functions such as human resources, education, communications, outreach, facilities/campus operations, events, volunteer or internship programs, or administrative services.
Experience strengthening management systems, roles, performance, and accountability. Experience with conservation, land stewardship, natural-resource management, agriculture, ranching, or working lands is desirable.

Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities
Strong interpersonal and communication skills; demonstrated ability to build trust, address difficult issues constructively, and work effectively across organizational levels.
Sound judgment and discretion, with the ability to make independent decisions within delegated authority while collaborating closely with executive leadership.
Ability to translate institutional priorities into clear roles, expectations, coordinated work, and follow-through across diverse functions.
A transparent, humble, and accountable management approach that respects expertise and helps others succeed across Archbold's diverse mission.

Work Environment & Physical Requirements
This is primarily an on-site, office-based leadership position with regular movement around Archbold's campus and periodic work at Buck Island Ranch or other Archbold locations. Work may occasionally involve outdoor conditions, uneven terrain, meetings or activities outside normal office settings, and local travel. Employees must be able to perform the essential functions of the position with or without reasonable accommodation.

This position offers a competitive annual salary ranging from $100,000 to $120,000, commensurate with experience, education, and qualifications. Starting salary will be determined based on the candidate's background and demonstrated expertise.

None

Description
The Northeast Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (NEAFWA), in partnership with the Wildlife Management Institute (WMI), seeks a qualified professional to provide regional coordination and project management support for a multi-state initiative to advance habitat connectivity across the Northeast. This position will strengthen the state-led institutional platform needed to coordinate connectivity work across the 13-state NEAFWA region. The coordinator will anchor the initiative within NEAFWA’s Northeast Landscape Conservation Committee, facilitate sustained engagement with federal agencies and other regional partners and networks, support the development of collaborative projects, and maintain consistent coordination among state agencies, federal agencies, nonprofit organizations, researchers, and other partners. The coordinator will help translate regional priorities into coordinated action while respecting the authorities and conservation priorities of individual states and participating organizations. The position will emphasize institutional coordination, partnership development, project management, and implementation support that builds upon the extensive connectivity efforts underway, rather than creating a separate regional planning process. 

The coordinator will be employed as a partner-based employee of WMI but will be supervised by a NEAFWA representative appointed by the NEAFWA President. The starting salary is negotiable based on education and experience. The position will be eligible for WMI 401(k) retirement and vacation benefits, and WMI will provide workers’ compensation, general liability protection, professional liability protection, unemployment insurance benefits, and medical, dental, and vision insurance benefits. 

Position Information 

Position title: Northeast Regional Connectivity Coordinator 
Location: Anywhere within the 13-state NEAFWA region 
Salary:  $65,000-$80,000 dependent on experience + benefits  

Classification: Full-time (salaried)
Start date: negotiable but ASAP
Duration: up to 3 years with potential for renewal
Application deadline: 10/15/26
Travel: Regional travel will be required. The amount and frequency of travel will vary based on project and partner needs.

 Introduction 

Habitat connectivity challenges extend across state and organizational boundaries and require coordinated regional planning and action. States and partners across the Northeast have developed important connectivity and corridor plans, data, projects, and collaborative partnerships such as the Staying Connected Initiative, but additional dedicated capacity is needed to further align these efforts, support enhanced collaboration, address barriers to project implementation, and advance shared priorities across this large region.  

The Northeast Regional Connectivity Coordinator will anchor this initiative within NEAFWA’s Northeast Landscape Conservation Committee. The coordinator will facilitate engagement among state and federal agencies and other regional partners, support the development of multi-state projects and funding proposals, help advance the Northeast Connectivity Framework, and maintain the coordination and project-management systems needed to move the regional effort forward. 

Duties and Responsibilities 

Support coordination among NEAFWA member states on regional habitat-connectivity priorities, projects, and funding opportunities. 
Serve as the primary staff support for connectivity work undertaken through NEAFWA’s Northeast Landscape Conservation Committee. 
Organize and facilitate meetings among state agencies, federal agencies, nonprofit organizations, and other regional partners, including preparing agendas, documenting decisions, and tracking follow-up actions. 
Maintain regular communication among participating states and partners to share information, identify common needs, and connect complementary efforts. 
Help states identify opportunities for multi-state collaboration and connect them with nonprofit and federal partners that can provide relevant expertise, capacity, or resources. 
Support the development of high impact collaborative, multi-state projects by clarifying objectives, partner roles, work plans, timelines, budgets, and next steps. 
Assist partners with concept papers, grant proposals, scopes of work, compliance, and other materials needed to advance priority projects. 
Track regional activities, project milestones, partner commitments, and funding opportunities, and prepare concise progress updates for NEAFWA and project partners. 
Coordinate with related regional and subregional connectivity efforts such as the Staying Connected Initiative to strengthen alignment and avoid duplication. 
Perform other related coordination and project management duties as needed to support the regional initiative. 
Minimum Qualifications 

A bachelor’s degree in wildlife biology, ecology, conservation science, natural resources management, environmental planning, public policy, geography, landscape ecology, or related field. A master’s degree is preferred. A combination of relevant education and substantial professional experience may be considered. 
At least 5 years of relevant professional experience in landscape-scale conservation, habitat connectivity, interagency coordination, collaborative conservation, project development, or a closely related field. 
Demonstrated experience coordinating complex initiatives involving multiple agencies, organizations, jurisdictions, or funding sources. 
Experience managing projects with multiple partners, deliverables, timelines, and decision-making structures. 
Strong written and oral communication skills, including the ability to communicate effectively with agency leaders, technical staff, nonprofit partners, researchers, funders, and other audiences. 
Demonstrated ability to work independently in a remote or distributed environment while maintaining consistent communication and accountability. 
Willingness and ability to travel within the Northeast region and occasionally elsewhere for meetings, workshops, and conferences. 
Preferred Qualifications and Selection Criteria

Knowledge of habitat connectivity, landscape conservation, ecological networks, wildlife movement, climate adaptation, or related conservation principles. 
Familiarity with state fish and wildlife agencies, federal conservation programs, and regional conservation partnerships in the Northeast.

Quality and clarity of written and oral communication.
